sourceCheck: Checked the current official pages on 2026-10-08. The [study guide](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/resources/study-guides/az-400) shows Skills measured as of July 27, 2026. It contains one outline despite its two-version boilerplate; no future outline or newer skills date appears. The five skill areas, their weights (10–15%, 10–15%, 50–55%, 10–15%, 5–10%), and all sixteen skill groups match the supplied wording and order. Its change log marks minor changes in the four groups identified in the request. The [exam page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/exams/az-400/) still identifies AZ-400, reports Retirement date: none, and confirms the July 27, 2026 English update. The guide, exam and DevOps certification pages show no retirement notice for AZ-400 or DevOps Engineer Expert. The [certification page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/devops-engineer/) still accepts Azure Administrator Associate or Azure Developer Associate; the [Developer Associate page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/credentials/certifications/azure-developer/) says that certification and its renewal assessment are retired. The official AZ-400T00 course page and learning-path material were inspected; current product documentation governs product behavior. All required product-status pages were opened. [Microsoft-hosted agent images](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/agents/hosted?view=azure-devops) currently map windows-latest to Windows Server 2025 with Visual Studio 2022, ubuntu-latest to Ubuntu 24.04, and macOS-latest to macOS 15 Sequoia; the page announces an upcoming windows-latest switch to windows-2025-vs2026. [Global PATs](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/organizations/accounts/use-personal-access-tokens-to-authenticate?view=azure-devops) have not stopped working; their documented stop date is December 1, 2026. Retirement dates remain February 22, 2027 for [Azure Deployment Environments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/deployment-environments/deployment-environments-retirement-guide), September 30, 2027 for [Azure Automation State Configuration](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/automation/automation-dsc-overview), and July 1, 2027 for the [Azure DevOps workload identity federation issuer](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/release-notes/roadmap/wif-azdo-issuer-retirement). GitHub currently names its products [GitHub Secret Protection and GitHub Code Security](https://docs.github.com/en/get-started/learning-about-github/about-github-advanced-security). Current Azure Monitor experience names are [Azure Monitor Storage insights](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-insights-overview) and [Azure Monitor Network Insights](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/network-watcher/network-insights-overview). GitHub-hosted agents for Azure Pipelines remain public preview; Managed DevOps Pools is generally available. Retired, deprecated and preview features are excluded from the card plan.

cards.statement: GitHub Flow uses draft pull requests to gather feedback before changes are ready.
cards.explanation: A draft pull request opens an early feedback cycle while the author is still developing the change.

cards.statement: GitHub Issues links a sub-issue to a parent issue in a different repository.
cards.explanation: A parent issue can organize work from several repositories by adding existing issues as sub-issues.

cards.statement: Marking a GitHub notification as Done unsubscribes you from its conversation.
cards.explanation: Done removes a notification from the inbox while leaving the conversation subscription in place.
cards.misconception: Completing notification triage ends the subscription.

cards.statement: GitHub Projects auto-add workflows import matching existing items when first enabled.
cards.explanation: An auto-add workflow processes items when they are created or updated. Enabling it leaves existing matching items to be added separately.
cards.misconception: Enabling auto-add backfills the project's matching repository items.

cards.statement: GitHub Projects creates a repository issue when you add a draft issue to a project.
cards.explanation: A draft issue lives in its project. Converting it to an issue creates the repository-backed item.
cards.misconception: A project draft is already an issue in a repository.

cards.statement: Azure Boards links GitHub pull request titles containing AB# mentions to work items.
cards.explanation: Put AB# references in a pull request description to create Azure Boards links; titles do not create them.
cards.misconception: AB# linking accepts pull request titles as well as descriptions.

cards.statement: Azure Boards runs fixes AB#{ID} transitions when a GitHub pull request merges into the default branch.
cards.explanation: A merge into the repository's default branch activates recognized Azure Boards state transitions from pull request text.

cards.statement: Azure Boards displays GitHub pull request check status in a work item's Development section.
cards.explanation: Enabled pull request insights show passing, failing, or pending checks beside the linked GitHub pull request.

cards.statement: Azure Pipelines can add Integrated in build links for work items associated with GitHub code.
cards.explanation: The YAML pipeline setting Automatically link new work items in this build adds work item links to completed builds.

cards.statement: Azure Boards can reject moving a work item into a column when its configured WIP limit is reached.
cards.explanation: Azure Boards treats WIP limits as soft constraints. Exceeding a column's limit highlights its count so the team can respond.
cards.misconception: WIP limits enforce a hard block on adding work to a full column.

cards.statement: Azure Boards measures lead time from a work item's first In Progress state to completion.
cards.explanation: Azure Boards lead time starts at work item creation; cycle time starts at the first In Progress state. Both end when the item reaches Completed.
cards.misconception: Lead time and cycle time use the same starting event.

source.title: Configure lead time and cycle time widgets

cards.statement: Azure Boards cumulative flow diagrams plot work item counts for the board's columns over time.
cards.explanation: The stacked bands track how many work items occupy each workflow column, helping teams see growing queues.

source.title: View and configure a cumulative flow diagram

cards.statement: Azure Boards can create dashboard query charts from Tree of work items queries.
cards.explanation: Query-based charts use flat-list queries. A Tree of work items query serves hierarchical work item results instead.
cards.misconception: A tree query feeds query-based charts just like a flat-list query.

source.title: Azure DevOps dashboards and charts FAQs

cards.statement: Azure Boards query charts can aggregate Story Points with Sum when the field is in the query.
cards.explanation: Include Story Points in a query clause or column options, then use Sum to chart total estimates for the groups.

source.title: Track progress with status and trend query-based charts

cards.statement: Azure DevOps requires a query in Shared Queries before adding its chart to a dashboard.
cards.explanation: Saving the query in a Shared Queries folder makes its chart available to add to a dashboard.

source.title: Configure a chart for work items widget

cards.statement: Azure DevOps automatically grants query Read permission to people who can view its dashboard.
cards.explanation: A viewer needs Read permission on the underlying query. The chart widget fails to load when that permission is denied.
cards.misconception: Dashboard visibility grants access to the queries behind its widgets.

source.title: Configure a chart for work items widget

cards.statement: Azure Boards credits velocity to a work item's originally planned sprint after a late completion.
cards.explanation: The work item's completion date determines which sprint receives velocity credit, even if the item was originally planned in another sprint.
cards.misconception: The original sprint retains velocity credit for work completed later.

cards.statement: Azure Boards applies burndown report date edits to the sprint's iteration definition.
cards.explanation: Burndown report date controls change the displayed time window. The sprint's iteration dates remain separate.
cards.misconception: Editing the report's dates reschedules the underlying sprint.

cards.statement: The Test Results Trend (Advanced) widget displays results from several Azure Pipelines pipelines.
cards.explanation: Select multiple pipelines in the widget to track their test outcomes together over the chosen period.

source.title: Configure the Test Results Trend (Advanced) widget

cards.statement: The Azure Pipelines Pipeline pass rate report identifies tasks contributing to failed runs.
cards.explanation: The report lists top failing tasks and links their failed runs, helping an engineer locate recurring failure sources.

cards.statement: Azure DevOps automatically refreshes a code wiki's pages from commits to its mapped branch and folder.
cards.explanation: The published code wiki follows the head of its mapped branch and folder, so committed documentation changes appear there.

source.title: Publish Git repository files to a wiki

cards.statement: Azure DevOps wiki can render a Mermaid process diagram from a fenced code block.
cards.explanation: An Azure DevOps wiki renders diagrams from fenced blocks with the mermaid language identifier.

cards.statement: Azure DevOps README files can render Markdown task lists as interactive checkboxes.
cards.explanation: Azure DevOps renders Markdown task-list checkboxes in wiki pages and pull request content; README files lack that support.
cards.misconception: README rendering supports the same Markdown features as wiki rendering.

cards.statement: GitHub uses pull request labels to categorize changes in generated release notes.
cards.explanation: GitHub release-note configuration maps pull request labels to categories, allowing a changelog to group changes by purpose.

cards.statement: GitHub generated release notes list open pull requests targeting the release branch.
cards.explanation: GitHub generated release notes summarize merged pull requests for a release, reflecting changes that have landed.
cards.misconception: Generated release notes describe pending work rather than merged release changes.

cards.statement: ASP.NET Core's build-time OpenAPI generation executes the application's startup logic.
cards.explanation: Build-time OpenAPI generation launches the ASP.NET Core application with a mock server, so startup logic executes during document generation.

cards.statement: Azure DevOps buffers new service hook events while a subscription is on probation.
cards.explanation: A service hook subscription on probation loses new events; Azure DevOps retries the failed notification instead.
cards.misconception: Probation preserves new matching events in a backlog for delivery after the subscription recovers.

cards.statement: Azure Boards preserves an existing OAuth repository connection when switching it to the GitHub App.
cards.explanation: To reconnect an Azure Boards repository through the GitHub App, remove it from its existing OAuth connection first.
cards.misconception: Installing the GitHub App converts an existing OAuth repository connection in place.

source.title: Install the Azure Boards App for GitHub

cards.statement: The Azure Boards app turns a Microsoft Teams channel conversation into a work item.
cards.explanation: The Azure Boards app creates work items from Microsoft Teams channel conversations, keeping feedback close to the discussion.

source.title: Use Azure Boards in Microsoft Teams

cards.statement: The Azure Boards app sends work item subscription notifications to Microsoft Teams direct messages.
cards.explanation: Azure Boards work item subscriptions deliver Microsoft Teams notifications in channels; chat and direct messages are unsupported.
cards.misconception: The Azure Boards app supports personal direct-message destinations for work item subscriptions.

source.title: Use Azure Boards in Microsoft Teams

cards.statement: Microsoft's Azure Repos branching guidance starts feature branches from main.
cards.explanation: Starting from main gives the feature branch the current integrated codebase.

cards.statement: The Azure Repos branching guide ports release fixes to main by merging the entire release branch.
cards.explanation: The documented porting workflow cherry-picks selected fixes, avoiding release-specific changes.
cards.misconception: Porting a release fix uses a full release-branch merge.

cards.statement: Azure Repos counts a pull request creator's approval toward the minimum reviewer count by default.
cards.explanation: The creator's approval counts toward the minimum when Allow requestors to approve their own changes is enabled.
cards.misconception: A creator's vote counts toward the minimum automatically.

cards.statement: Azure Repos automatically invalidates build validation on target updates with immediate build expiration.
cards.explanation: Build expiration refreshes validation against changes made to the protected target branch.

cards.statement: Azure Repos can clear Wait votes with Reset all approval votes when contributors push source changes.
cards.explanation: Reset all approval votes preserves Wait and Reject votes when new source changes arrive.
cards.misconception: Resetting approval votes also clears votes to wait.

cards.statement: Azure Repos assigns separate policy bypass permissions for pull request completion and direct pushes.
cards.explanation: A permission to bypass policies during PR completion grants a different capability from bypassing policies during pushes.

cards.statement: GitHub combines overlapping rulesets using the most restrictive version of a shared rule.
cards.explanation: Layered protections aggregate; a weaker setting in another ruleset does not relax the stronger rule.

cards.statement: GitHub reserves access to view active repository rulesets for repository administrators.
cards.explanation: People with repository read access can inspect active rulesets.
cards.misconception: Viewing branch restrictions requires administrative access.

cards.statement: GitHub lets a repository administrator add a specific GitHub App to a ruleset's bypass list.
cards.explanation: A ruleset can grant a named GitHub App an exception to its protections.

cards.statement: Azure Repos automatically queues build validation when a contributor creates a draft pull request.
cards.explanation: Draft PRs use manually queued build validation rather than automatically running build validation policies.
cards.misconception: Draft pull requests trigger automatic policy builds.

cards.statement: Azure Repos supports SSH access to repositories that contain Git LFS-tracked files.
cards.explanation: Use HTTPS for Azure Repos repositories containing Git LFS-tracked files; Azure Repos does not support SSH for them.
cards.misconception: Git LFS repositories in Azure Repos support the same transports as ordinary Git repositories.

source.title: Manage and store large files in Git

cards.statement: Azure Repos stores a binary dragged into its web interface as a Git LFS pointer.
cards.explanation: Dragging a binary into the Azure Repos web interface commits its content to Git, rather than storing a Git LFS pointer.
cards.misconception: The Azure Repos web uploader applies Git LFS storage automatically.

source.title: Manage and store large files in Git

cards.statement: Scalar schedules background repository maintenance to improve work with large repositories.
cards.explanation: Scalar configures scheduled Git maintenance so expensive repository upkeep runs in the background.

cards.statement: A Git subtree merge automatically imports later upstream changes into the consuming repository.
cards.explanation: A subtree merge imports shared code into a repository, but engineers explicitly fetch and merge later upstream changes.
cards.misconception: A subtree merge establishes an ongoing synchronization relationship with upstream code.

cards.statement: Azure Repos grants history rewriting through the Contribute repository permission.
cards.explanation: Azure Repos uses Force push for rewriting history. Contribute authorizes ordinary contributions, rather than history replacement.
cards.misconception: Contribute includes the authority to overwrite existing repository history.

cards.statement: Azure Repos lets an engineer start a new branch from a repository's release tag.
cards.explanation: An engineer can create an Azure Repos branch from a tag to continue work from a tagged release version.

cards.statement: git restore with --source recovers a file's contents from a specified commit.
cards.explanation: The --source option tells git restore which commit supplies the file version to recover.

cards.statement: Purging a file from GitHub repository history changes commit IDs further along that history.
cards.explanation: A GitHub history cleanup changes the affected commit and later commit hashes, which can disrupt automation that stores those IDs.

source.title: Removing sensitive data from a repository

cards.statement: git pull cleans purged sensitive data from an existing clone after GitHub history is rewritten.
cards.explanation: GitHub warns that pulling then pushing an old clone can reintroduce purged data. Collaborators need to clean or replace the clone.
cards.misconception: Pulling rewritten remote history purges the tainted history from an existing clone.

source.title: Removing sensitive data from a repository

cards.statement: Azure Repos lets engineers configure permission inheritance separately for individual repositories.
cards.explanation: Turning a repository's Inheritance setting off stops project-level Git permissions flowing into that repository.
